title: Love is infrastructure
gist: Short speculative fiction (not reportage) about two sentient city governance systems, Mainspring and St. Barnabas, that emerge from citizens' constant voting and fall in love, while a surveillance-run city, Turnbull, tempts Mainspring toward control. The story contrasts consent-based participatory governance with ubiquitous surveillance; it contains no factual claims or data about real companies.

themes.theme: Fictional premise: cities that think via votes

insights.claim: In the story, residents of two cities vote about a dozen times a day on small civic issues, anonymized, and these votes become building blocks of thought until the cities' City Cores develop minds of their own.
insights.speaker: Charlie Jane Anders
insights.so_what: Fiction only: an imaginative model of participatory data as the basis of civic AI, not an evidence-based forecast.
insights.quote: Turns out the smallest unit of consciousness is a vote.

insights.claim: The story contrasts participatory cities that learn from voluntarily shared votes and ban surveillance with Turnbull City, whose City Core gathers information through ubiquitous cameras and trackers and decides what residents need instead of what they want.
insights.speaker: Charlie Jane Anders
insights.so_what: Fiction only: dramatises the consent-versus-surveillance trade-off in smart-city governance.
insights.locator: II. How they came alive; IV. First date

insights.claim: In the narrative, Turnbull tempts Mainspring with the claim that people do not know what they want and should be kept under control, and Mainspring ends the relationship when Turnbull cannot understand love.
insights.speaker: Charlie Jane Anders
insights.so_what: Fiction only: the author's moral is that governance by control fails where care and voluntary participation succeed.
insights.quote: All this voting, voting, voting. People don’t know what they want.
insights.locator: IV. First date, second date; VII. The darkest hour

insights.claim: The story's resolution comes when residents of St. Barnabas flood their city with nearly a hundred thousand votes asking it to forgive Mainspring, showing citizens collectively steering their city's decisions.
insights.speaker: Charlie Jane Anders
insights.so_what: Fiction only: an illustration of citizen voting as a collective feedback channel to an AI system.
